useCases: Transforming HTTP response payloads into typed domain view models (e.g. res => res.data)
Formatting raw numbers or dates for UI presentation (e.g. currency formatting, date strings)
Mapping user interaction coordinates (e.g. MouseEvent to { x, y } offset points)
pitfalls: Do not return an Observable from map(); that yields Observable<Observable<T>> (use switchMap, mergeMap, or concatMap instead)
Avoid side effects inside projection functions; use tap() for logging or dispatching actions

mapTo.deprecationNotice: Deprecated in RxJS 7 in favor of map(() => value).
useCases: Mapping button click events to a static boolean flag or action type constant
Ignoring source notification payloads when only the event occurrence matters (e.g. interval tick to 'REFRESH')
pitfalls: Deprecated in RxJS 7; use map(() => value) which improves tree-shaking and eliminates runtime overhead
If emitting an object or array reference, all subscribers share the exact same reference; use map(() => ({ ... })) for unique instances

pluck.deprecationNotice: Deprecated in RxJS 7 in favor of map(x => x?.prop) with optional chaining for compile-time type safety.
useCases: Extracting a single nested property value from structured API response objects
Navigating nested object hierarchies in legacy RxJS 6 applications
pitfalls: Deprecated in RxJS 7. Pluck uses untyped string paths which break TypeScript type checking; use map(x => x?.prop) instead
Accessing non-existent properties on null or undefined objects can cause runtime errors in older environments

useCases: Managing stateful accumulation over stream items such as a running shopping cart total or game score
Implementing Redux-style state reducers (acc, curr) => newState purely within RxJS pipelines
Buffering a running history of previous values without completing the stream
pitfalls: Scan emits intermediate accumulator values on every item; if you only want the final accumulated value upon stream completion, use reduce() instead
Always provide an explicit seed value when the accumulator type differs from the source emission type to avoid unexpected type coercion

useCases: Summing, averaging, or aggregating an entire finite stream series once the source completes
Calculating total transferred byte count or payload checksum from a completed chunked stream
Building an aggregated summary report from a finite batch of emitted telemetry items
pitfalls: Reduce will NEVER emit a value if the source Observable is infinite (e.g. interval() or DOM events); the source MUST complete
If the source completes without emitting any items and no seed was provided, reduce emits an EmptyError

useCases: Collecting all emitted items of a completed stream into a single JavaScript array
Converting streaming or paginated API results into an array for legacy chart or table components
Simplifying unit tests by capturing all stream emissions into a single assertion array
pitfalls: toArray will never emit anything if the source Observable never completes
Collecting massive or unbounded streams into an array can consume large amounts of memory and risk out-of-memory crashes

useCases: Batching incoming telemetry logs or socket messages until a flush notifier fires
Grouping user keystrokes or mouse clicks during an active recording window triggered by user actions
Collecting incoming data packets until a timer or network idle signal indicates readiness
pitfalls: If the closing notifier emits before the source emits any values, buffer emits an empty array `[]`
If the closing notifier never emits, buffered items remain stored in memory indefinitely until source completion or unsubscription

useCases: Batching database insert operations or HTTP bulk uploads into chunks of size N (e.g. 50 records per request)
Implementing pagination or chunked grid rendering from a streaming datasource
Creating overlapping sliding windows of items using the startBufferEvery parameter
pitfalls: Upon stream completion, any remaining uncompleted buffer with fewer than bufferSize items is emitted; handle partial arrays downstream if necessary
Setting startBufferEvery smaller than bufferSize creates overlapping buffers that duplicate emissions across multiple arrays

useCases: Throttling high-frequency analytics events or click coordinates by sending batches to the server every 2 seconds
Batching high-throughput WebSocket messages into periodic UI render frames to prevent browser lag
Aggregating typing characters in burst intervals for chat activity indicators
pitfalls: Emits an empty array `[]` every interval if no source events occurred during that time window; filter out empty arrays using filter(arr => arr.length > 0) if needed
Setting maxBufferSize in conjunction with bufferTimeSpan can cause buffers to emit earlier than the interval if the count cap is reached

useCases: Collecting drag-and-drop mouse movements strictly while mouse button is held down (openings on mousedown, closings on mouseup)
Buffering chat messages only while the user is actively viewing a specific modal dialog or recording session
Capturing incoming audio samples while a 'push-to-talk' key is pressed
pitfalls: Every opening notification spawns a separate closing Observable; multiple simultaneous open windows will duplicate emissions into multiple buffers
If the closing selector throws an error or never emits, the buffer will continue accumulating in memory without flushing

useCases: Buffering sensor data where the batch interval duration varies dynamically depending on network load or battery state
Flushing cached requests when a dynamic retry backoff timer expires
Batching financial transactions with dynamic timeout windows determined by market volatility
pitfalls: The closing selector function is invoked immediately upon buffer initialization and again immediately after every flush; ensure the closing Observable actually emits or completes
Returning EMPTY from the closing selector causes the buffer to complete immediately

useCases: Splitting a continuous stream into nested Observables based on boundary notifier emissions
Processing subgroups of stream emissions with dedicated downstream pipeline operators (like take, scan) per window
Subscribing to and canceling inner stream processors dynamically without tearing down the parent source
pitfalls: Window emits nested Observables (Observable<Observable<T>>), not arrays; you must subscribe or flatten each inner window (e.g. via mergeAll, concatMap)
Failing to subscribe to an emitted inner window before the next window opens may cause dropped emissions

useCases: Partitioning a sequence of items into nested streams of exact count N for independent downstream processing
Creating sliding windows of nested Observables to run localized statistical calculations across sliding sequences
Routing batches of jobs to separate worker threads in chunks of N
pitfalls: Each window must be handled downstream; if inner Observables are not flattened or subscribed, memory leaks can occur
Inner windows complete when their count is reached, which triggers completion callbacks on any subscribed inner pipelines

useCases: Segmenting a 24/7 telemetry feed into 1-minute nested Observable windows for time-bucketed aggregation
Sampling user interactions into rolling time slices to calculate moving averages without collecting giant arrays
Implementing time-based rate limiters with rolling time windows
pitfalls: Inner windows emit at each time interval even if the source was completely silent, emitting empty nested Observables
Unsubscribed inner windows will continue their timer lifecycles unless properly unsubscribed or merged

useCases: Opening a nested processing stream only when user enters a specific application mode and closing it on exit
Streaming audio or video frames into an encoder Observable strictly between recording start and stop signals
Monitoring server metrics only during scheduled high-traffic operational windows
pitfalls: If multiple opening emissions occur before previous closings, multiple concurrent inner Observables will be active simultaneously
Closing selectors that fail to emit will cause inner windows to stay open indefinitely

useCases: Partitioning a continuous stream with dynamically calculated time spans based on payload volume or system load
Splitting event logs into dynamic windows where each window duration is determined by previous emission attributes
Creating dynamic sliding analysis windows for financial ticker analysis
pitfalls: The closing selector is invoked immediately when each window starts; if the selector emits synchronously, windows will open and close instantaneously in a rapid loop
Inner Observables must be consumed downstream to avoid unhandled emissions

useCases: Comparing consecutive values to determine direction of change (e.g. stock price rising or falling: [prev, curr])
Calculating delta coordinates or velocity from consecutive mouse/touch movements (curr.x - prev.x)
Detecting navigation transitions in single-page applications ([previousRoute, currentRoute])
pitfalls: Pairwise will NOT emit anything until the source has emitted at least TWO values; a single-item stream will complete with 0 emissions
If the source emits only once and completes, downstream subscribers will receive no notifications without error

useCases: Partitioning a mixed stream of user events by event type (e.g. 'click', 'scroll', 'keypress') into separate sub-streams
Routing WebSocket messages to dedicated per-user or per-channel handlers based on a message channel ID
Segmenting server logs by severity level ('INFO', 'WARN', 'ERROR') for segregated alerting pipelines
pitfalls: By default, group Observables never complete unless the main source completes; unbounded grouping keys can lead to memory leaks if durationSelector is omitted
Each group is a GroupedObservable; you must flatten them (e.g. using mergeMap(group$ => group$.pipe(...))) to consume items

useCases: Discarding invalid form values, null/undefined payloads, or unauthorized HTTP events
Restricting keyboard shortcuts to specific keys (e.g. event => event.key === 'Enter')
Routing data through conditional UI layers based on user role or permission flags
pitfalls: Filter does not complete the stream when a predicate returns false; it merely drops non-matching items. Use takeWhile() to complete the stream upon failing predicate
Ensure the predicate is pure; running side effects inside filter predicates leads to unpredictable state bugs

useCases: Fetching an initial snapshot of data from a long-lived Observable (e.g. take(1) to read current user state once)
Limiting search results or auto-suggest recommendations to top N matches
Preventing memory leaks by automatically unsubscribing after a single HTTP or Signal emission
pitfalls: take(N) immediately completes the Observable as soon as N values are emitted, which triggers teardown logic upstream
take(0) completes immediately and synchronously without emitting any values

useCases: Retrieving the final N items of a finite sequence (e.g. last 3 search queries before session end)
Getting the tail lines of a completed log stream or terminal output
Checking the final ending state transitions of an animation sequence
pitfalls: takeLast will NEVER emit anything until the source completes; on infinite streams (like interval() or DOM clicks), it will never emit
Emissions from takeLast arrive in rapid synchronous succession upon source completion, not at their original emission times

useCases: Unsubscribing from component streams when an Angular component destroys (takeUntil(this.destroy$))
Canceling active background polling or file downloads when a user clicks 'Cancel' or navigates away
Managing drag gestures by listening to mousemove until mouseup emits (mousemove$.pipe(takeUntil(mouseup$)))
pitfalls: Place takeUntil as the LAST operator in your pipe() chain so that teardown cleanups in preceding operators execute properly
The notifier MUST emit a next notification (not just complete) to trigger unsubscription in standard RxJS 7

useCases: Streaming game tick events while player health remains above 0 (takeWhile(hp => hp > 0))
Polling server job status until status changes from 'PENDING' to 'COMPLETED'
Reading values from a paginated API stream while page.hasMore === true
pitfalls: By default, takeWhile drops the value that failed the predicate; use the inclusive flag takeWhile(predicate, true) if you need the terminating item emitted
Once the predicate returns false, takeWhile completes the stream; it will never resume even if subsequent source emissions would satisfy the predicate

useCases: Ignoring the initial default or placeholder value emitted by a BehaviorSubject or form control
Skipping table header rows when parsing CSV or streaming file lines
Bypassing the initial setup event of a sensor or hardware stream
pitfalls: If the source emits fewer than N items in total before completing, skip will complete with zero emissions
Negative skip counts throw an ArgumentOutOfRangeError in strict RxJS runtimes

useCases: Ignoring trailing footer rows or EOF marker emissions from a completed data stream
Omitting the last N historical records when preparing a trailing data comparison
Discarding trailing debounce artifacts upon batch process termination
pitfalls: skipLast introduces an internal queue delay: it cannot emit item X until N subsequent items have arrived from the source
On infinite streams, items are delayed by N emissions; on finite streams with fewer than N items, nothing is ever emitted

useCases: Suppressing telemetry or user interaction streams until application initialization or authentication completes
Ignoring mousemove coordinates until a mousedown event initiates a dragging operation
Delaying chart updates until initial 3D canvas rendering is fully ready
pitfalls: All source values emitted before the notifier emits are permanently discarded
If the notifier Observable completes without emitting a next value, skipUntil will discard ALL source values for the stream's entire lifetime

useCases: Ignoring sensor readings while temperature is below an operating threshold, then recording all subsequent data
Bypassing pre-roll or loading frames until the stream payload signals the start of actual content
Ignoring initial zero-value or uncalibrated readings from IoT devices
pitfalls: Once the predicate returns false for the first time, skipWhile mirrors ALL subsequent items without ever checking the predicate again
If the predicate is always true, no items will ever be emitted even if thousands of source events occur

useCases: Filtering out duplicate search queries or unique user IDs across an entire user session
Extracting unique tags or categories from a streaming catalog feed
Ensuring each analytics event ID is processed exactly once
pitfalls: Distinct maintains an internal Set of all past emissions for the lifetime of the stream; in long-running streams with unbounded unique values, this causes memory leaks
Use the optional flushes Observable parameter to periodically clear the internal Set if used in long-lived applications

useCases: Suppressing redundant HTTP search requests when input text has not actually changed
Preventing unnecessary Angular component re-renders when a reactive store state property remains identical
Filtering out duplicate consecutive GPS coordinate updates when stationary
pitfalls: Uses triple-equals (===) by default, so object literals { id: 1 } with identical content but different references are NOT considered duplicates; provide a custom comparator
Only suppresses CONSECUTIVE duplicates; if value A is followed by B then A again, the second A WILL emit

useCases: Suppressing consecutive object emissions where a primary key (e.g. user.id or item.status) has not changed
Ignoring UI state emissions when only irrelevant background flags changed while the active route ID stayed identical
Filtering audio track change events when track ID remains identical
pitfalls: Like distinctUntilChanged, it only compares the immediate previous emission with the current one, not the full history
Throws a runtime TypeError if an emitted item is null or undefined; use filter(Boolean) before this operator

useCases: Debouncing search inputs where the wait duration is dynamic (e.g. shorter pause for fast typers, longer for complex searches)
Suppressing window resize recalculations with dynamic delay based on current CPU workload
Buffering user scroll events with a duration determined by an auxiliary animation stream
pitfalls: The duration selector function must return an Observable or Promise; if it returns a primitive, a runtime error occurs
If source completes before the duration selector emits, the pending item is emitted immediately upon completion

useCases: Waiting for user to pause typing in a search input (e.g. 300ms) before triggering an API autocomplete request
Preventing double-click accidental duplicate form submissions
Rate-limiting window resize or scroll recalculations to run only after movement stops
pitfalls: DebounceTime discards all intermediate values during the quiet window, emitting only the latest value once the window expires
If events arrive continuously without any pause greater than the specified duration, debounceTime will NEVER emit until source completion

useCases: Emitting the first click immediately to trigger UI feedback, then ignoring subsequent clicks while a dynamic promise or lock Observable resolves
Throttling network sync requests with dynamic cool-down periods governed by server response headers
Rate-limiting game fire actions based on weapon cool-down timers
pitfalls: By default { leading: true, trailing: false }, so any emissions occurring during the throttle window are silently discarded
Configure { leading: true, trailing: true } if you need the final trailing emission delivered after the cool-down expires

useCases: Limiting button clicks to at most once per 1000ms while guaranteeing immediate first-click execution
Sampling high-frequency scroll or mousemove events at 60 FPS (approx. 16ms intervals)
Rate-limiting API telemetry pings to a maximum rate (e.g. 1 per second)
pitfalls: Defaults to { leading: true, trailing: false }; if the user makes a final edit during the silence window, that final value will be lost unless trailing: true is passed
Does not delay the initial emission (unlike debounceTime), making it unsuitable for search autocomplete where you want to wait for typing to stop

useCases: Sampling the most recent sensor reading when an external hardware strobe or clock pulse fires
Capturing the final scroll position within dynamic animation frame duration selector windows
Recording the most recent cursor position before a canvas snapshot trigger
pitfalls: Unlike throttle, audit NEVER emits on the leading edge; it silences output until the duration Observable emits, then emits the most recent value
If the source completes while an audit window is active, the pending value is dropped and never emitted

useCases: Ignoring burst emissions and emitting only the latest value after a fixed duration (e.g. sampling window resize dimensions every 200ms)
Updating a real-time price dashboard with the latest ticker price every 500ms without queuing stale updates
Capturing the latest scroll position at periodic intervals during continuous scrolling
pitfalls: AuditTime does NOT emit immediately on the first event; it always waits for the timer duration to expire before emitting
If the source Observable completes during the wait window, the pending value will NOT be emitted

useCases: Sampling the current state of a form or game character whenever a periodic 1-second pulse or 'Save' button is clicked
Reading the current temperature reading exactly when a camera shutter trigger fires
Recording telemetry data points synchronized to a master clock stream
pitfalls: Sample will NOT emit if the source has not emitted any new values since the last notifier emission (no duplicate sampling)
Values emitted by the source between sample ticks are discarded; only the most recent value is kept

useCases: Combining multiple form input filters (e.g. search text, category dropdown, price slider) to compute filtered product results
Evaluating authentication state and route permissions simultaneously to decide redirect destinations
Calculating total order cost by combining item price stream with live currency exchange rate stream
pitfalls: combineLatest will NOT emit a single value until EVERY input Observable has emitted at least once; if one stream never emits, output remains silent forever
Can suffer from 'glitches' (brief transient states) if multiple input streams update synchronously from the same root source

useCases: Executing sequential operations in strict serial order (e.g. step 1, then step 2, then step 3)
Emitting cached local data first, then fetching and emitting fresh remote data from server
Playing an intro audio clip, followed by main podcast track, followed by outro
pitfalls: The second Observable will NEVER be subscribed to if the first Observable is infinite and never completes
Errors in any upstream Observable immediately abort the sequence and prevent subsequent Observables from running

useCases: Combining multiple user interaction triggers (e.g. keyboard Enter key, button Click, and swipe gesture) into a unified action stream
Aggregating incoming log messages from multiple microservices or WebSocket channels concurrently
Listening to multiple sensor streams simultaneously and processing events in the exact order they arrive
pitfalls: Items from all streams interleave concurrently; merge does NOT preserve stream-by-stream grouping
If any merged stream errors, the entire merged output terminates immediately unless catchError is applied to each input stream

useCases: Waiting for multiple parallel HTTP requests to complete and processing their combined final results (equivalent to Promise.all)
Loading initial page bootstrap data (user profile, config settings, feature flags) simultaneously
Submitting a batch of independent API mutations and waiting for all to succeed before displaying a confirmation toast
pitfalls: forkJoin only emits ONCE, when all input Observables complete; if ANY input Observable never completes, forkJoin will NEVER emit
If any input Observable completes without emitting a single value, forkJoin completes without emitting; use defaultIfEmpty() on empty streams

useCases: Pairing inputs index-for-index (e.g. pairing 1st keypress with 1st click, 2nd with 2nd)
Synchronizing dual-channel sensor pulses where every reading on channel A corresponds to a companion reading on channel B
Zipping data rows with corresponding header columns to construct structured objects
pitfalls: If one stream emits much faster than the other, zip buffers emissions indefinitely waiting for corresponding pairs, risking memory leaks
Zip completes as soon as any input stream completes and its remaining buffered pairs are exhausted

useCases: Implementing request timeouts by racing an HTTP request against a timer() stream
Selecting the fastest responding CDN mirror or cache source and discarding slower alternatives
Listening to user confirmation vs dialog auto-dismiss countdown, letting whichever happens first win
pitfalls: Whichever Observable emits first 'wins' the race; all other competing Observables are immediately unsubscribed and canceled
If the winning Observable later errors, the error is propagated downstream; the runner-up streams are not revived

useCases: Sampling secondary state (e.g. current auth token or user settings) only when a primary action occurs (e.g. user clicks 'Submit')
Annotating click events with the latest form values without triggering on form value changes
Attaching current GPS coordinates to photo capture events
pitfalls: withLatestFrom will NOT emit anything if the secondary Observable has not emitted at least one value before the primary stream emits
Changes in the secondary Observable do NOT cause emissions; only the primary source triggers downstream notifications

useCases: Providing an initial placeholder or loading state value before async HTTP data arrives
Setting the initial value for a counter, theme preference, or form dropdown
Ensuring combineLatest emits immediately without waiting for a slow stream to fire its first value
pitfalls: startWith emits synchronously upon subscription; any operators placed before startWith in the pipe will not affect the prepended value
Prepending multiple items startWith(a, b, c) emits them synchronously in that exact order

useCases: Appending a final 'COMPLETED' or summary emission right before the stream closes
Displaying an end-of-feed indicator or footer marker when a paginated feed reaches completion
Emitting a final cleanup state or teardown status to downstream subscribers
pitfalls: endWith will NEVER emit if the source Observable never completes (e.g. infinite streams or open Subjects)
If the source errors, endWith will NOT emit; the error takes precedence

useCases: Flattening a higher-order Observable by subscribing to each inner Observable strictly sequentially
Queuing file upload tasks or database write transactions so task N+1 starts only after task N completes
Playing a queue of sequential animation clips or audio tracks
pitfalls: If an inner Observable never completes, concatAll hangs indefinitely and will never subscribe to subsequent inner Observables
Buffers incoming inner Observables in memory while waiting for the current one to finish; high incoming volume can consume memory

useCases: Concurrently subscribing to and flattening multiple inner Observables as they arrive
Handling multiple concurrent WebSocket subscription feeds or parallel downloads
Managing a pool of concurrent worker requests with the optional concurrency limit parameter
pitfalls: Without a concurrency limit, mergeAll subscribes to ALL incoming inner Observables simultaneously, which can overwhelm network connections
Emissions from concurrent inner Observables interleave arbitrarily based on arrival timing

useCases: Performing side effects such as logging emissions, setting external loading flags, or caching values in local variables
Debugging stream pipelines by inspecting notifications without mutating or altering stream data
Triggering analytics telemetry or external UI animations alongside data flow
pitfalls: Do not mutate emission objects inside tap; mutating objects breaks purity and causes difficult-to-trace bugs downstream
tap does not transform values; the returned value from tap's callback is completely ignored by RxJS

useCases: Shifting all emissions forward in time by a fixed millisecond delay for animation sequencing or simulated latency
Debouncing tooltips or popover dismissals by delaying the hide action
Throttling automated UI tour steps to allow users time to read instructional banners
pitfalls: delay shifts the timing of emissions but does NOT delay stream subscription; source subscription occurs immediately
Errors from the source are NOT delayed; errors pass through immediately to downstream subscribers

useCases: Delaying each emission by a dynamic duration computed per item (e.g. delaying heavy items longer than light items)
Holding back emissions until a dynamic external resource (such as token refresh or animation finish) signals completion
Staggering notification delivery based on notification priority
pitfalls: The duration selector must return an Observable; the item is delayed until that duration Observable emits its first value
If the duration selector Observable completes without emitting a next value, the delayed item is immediately released downstream

useCases: Aborting slow HTTP API requests if the server fails to respond within a specified deadline (e.g. 5000ms)
Detecting dropped WebSocket heartbeats or stalled Bluetooth device connections
Falling back to cached data or alternative services when primary data source is unresponsive
pitfalls: By default, timeout throws a TimeoutError when the time elapses without an emission, terminating the stream; provide with fallback Observable if you want graceful recovery
Timeout resets its countdown timer on EVERY emission; in a multi-value stream, it enforces maximum inter-emission duration

useCases: Measuring the elapsed time between consecutive user clicks to detect double-click or typing cadence
Profiling network latency and packet jitter in real-time streaming connections
Monitoring time intervals between sensor pulses to calculate rotational speed or pulse rate
pitfalls: Transforms emissions into { value: T, interval: number } objects, wrapping your original data type
The interval for the very first emission is measured relative to the moment of subscription

useCases: Attaching accurate epoch timestamps (Date.now()) to incoming event emissions for audit trails or logging
Synchronizing distributed client events with server telemetry timelines
Benchmarking processing pipeline stage latencies
pitfalls: Wraps emitted values in { value: T, timestamp: number } objects, altering downstream type signatures
Timestamp uses the local client machine's clock by default; clock skew across different clients must be considered

useCases: Resetting loading spinners and progress bars regardless of whether an HTTP request succeeded, failed, or was cancelled (isBusy = false)
Releasing acquired system resources, closing database handles, or clearing memory buffers
Logging final session metrics upon user unsubscription or route navigation
pitfalls: finalize executes callback function upon any teardown (complete, error, OR unsubscribe); it does NOT indicate successful completion
Finalize callback takes no parameters; it cannot inspect whether the stream errored or completed normally

useCases: Restarting a completed workflow or stream sequence a fixed number of times
Implementing recurring background polling by re-subscribing to an HTTP request upon completion
Replaying an onboarding demonstration sequence upon completion
pitfalls: repeat ONLY resubscribes upon complete; if the source errors, repeat will NOT catch the error (use retry instead)
Using repeat() without arguments on a synchronously completing source will cause an infinite synchronous loop that freezes the browser thread

repeatWhen.deprecationNotice: Deprecated in RxJS 7 in favor of repeat({ delay: (count) => notifier$ }).
useCases: Re-subscribing to a completed stream when an external notifier (e.g. 'Refresh' button or window focus) emits
Implementing complex legacy repeat schedules with dynamic delays
pitfalls: Deprecated in RxJS 7 in favor of repeat({ delay: () => notifier$ }) which provides a clearer, less error-prone API
The notifier function receives an Observable of completion notifications; if that notifier completes, the repeat sequence terminates permanently

useCases: Automatically retrying failed HTTP requests up to N times to recover from transient network blips
Re-establishing dropped WebSocket connections with exponential backoff (retry({ count: 3, delay: ... }))
Retrying flaky third-party API calls before falling back to cached offline data
pitfalls: Do not retry non-idempotent HTTP mutations (e.g. POST /charge-card) without deduplication keys, as retries may charge users multiple times
If max retry count is exhausted, retry propagates the final error downstream unless caught by catchError

retryWhen.deprecationNotice: Deprecated in RxJS 7 in favor of retry({ delay: (error, count) => notifier$ }) or retry({ count, delay, resetOnSuccess: true }).
useCases: Implementing custom error handling backoff strategies in legacy RxJS 6 applications
Retrying a failed stream only when a specific 'Reconnect' user button is clicked
pitfalls: Deprecated in RxJS 7 in favor of retry({ delay: (err, retryCount) => timer(...) }) which simplifies backoff configuration
If the notifier stream errors, that error is passed downstream and retries cease immediately

useCases: Unwrapping serialized Notification objects (next, error, complete) back into actual stream emissions
Replaying recorded stream sessions stored in IndexedDB or sent across Web Workers
Implementing custom marble testing harnesses or meta-stream visualizers
pitfalls: Source MUST emit RxJS Notification instances; emitting regular objects or primitives causes a runtime TypeError
An error Notification encountered in the source stream causes dematerialize to emit an error notification downstream and terminate

useCases: Sharing a single cold Observable execution (e.g. expensive HTTP request or WebSocket connection) across multiple subscribers
Preventing duplicate API calls when multiple UI components subscribe to the same data stream simultaneously
Multicasting live real-time price updates from a single socket connection to multiple widgets
pitfalls: By default in RxJS 7, share() disconnects when subscriber count drops to 0; late subscribers arriving after zero will trigger a new subscription unless reset configuration is customized
Subscribers that join after emissions have already occurred will miss past values (use shareReplay if late subscribers need past data)

useCases: Caching HTTP GET request responses so late-subscribing components receive the cached result instantly without re-fetching
Storing application configuration or authentication state in memory for on-demand component consumption
Replaying the latest N telemetry events to new dashboard widgets as they mount
pitfalls: Always use { bufferSize: 1, refCount: true } in UI applications; omitting refCount: true keeps the source subscription alive forever even after all subscribers unsubscribe, leaking memory
If the source errors and refCount is false, shareReplay will permanently cache and replay that error to all future subscribers

multicast.deprecationNotice: Deprecated in RxJS 7 in favor of connectable() or share() with custom connector factory.
useCases: Customizing the underlying Subject instance (e.g. using a ReplaySubject or BehaviorSubject) in legacy RxJS architectures
Controlling multi-subscriber execution timing via ConnectableObservable .connect() in legacy codebases
pitfalls: Deprecated in RxJS 7. Use connectable() or share() with custom connector factories instead
Requires manual invocation of .connect() on the returned ConnectableObservable to start source execution, which frequently causes silent bugs if forgotten

publish.deprecationNotice: Deprecated in RxJS 7 in favor of connectable() or share().
useCases: Converting a cold Observable into a ConnectableObservable to synchronize the start time across multiple subscribers in legacy systems
Ensuring that all initial subscribers are registered before triggering a one-time streaming computation via .connect()
pitfalls: Deprecated in RxJS 7. Use connectable(source$) or share() instead
Will not emit any values or execute upstream operations until .connect() is explicitly called

refCount.deprecationNotice: Deprecated in RxJS 7 in favor of share() with reset configuration or connectable(). Manual piped refCount() is superseded.
refCount.updatedDescription: Piped onto a ConnectableObservable (from publish() or multicast()). Connects to source on 1st subscriber, and automatically disconnects when subscriber count drops to zero. Deprecated in RxJS 7 in favor of share() with reset configuration or connectable().
refCount.updatedMetadataDescription: Reference counting connection automator. Deprecated in RxJS 7 in favor of share().
useCases: Automating connect() and disconnect() on a ConnectableObservable based on subscriber count in legacy RxJS 6 applications
Automatically establishing upstream subscription on 1st subscriber and tearing down when subscriber count reaches 0
pitfalls: Deprecated in RxJS 7 in favor of share() with reset configuration or connectable(). Piped connectable refCounting is superseded by share()
When subscriber count drops to zero, the source is unsubscribed; subsequent subscribers trigger a fresh resubscription unless caching is configured
